Later that night, Jesus walks on the Sea of Galilee. Peter briefly walks on water too but sinks due to fear, crying out to be saved. The disciples worship Jesus as the Son of God.

entries.author: The Blessed Bible Study Guide
entries.text:
**Tradition and Defilement, and the Faith of a Canaanite Woman**

**Themes:** Hypocrisy, Purity of heart, Gentile faith, Compassion, Miraculous provision

**Outline:**
I. Traditions and Commandments (15:1-9)
II. What Defiles a Person (15:10-20)
III. The Faith of a Canaanite Woman (15:21-28)
IV. Jesus Heals Many (15:29-31)
V. Jesus Feeds the Four Thousand (15:32-39)

**Summary:**
Jesus rebukes the Pharisees for elevating human tradition above God's commandments, teaching that true defilement comes from wicked thoughts in the heart, not unwashed hands. Withdrawing to Tyre and Sidon, he tests and then rewards the persistent, humble faith of a Canaanite woman by healing her demon-oppressed daughter. Returning near the Sea of Galilee, he heals many and miraculously feeds a crowd of 4,000 men (plus women and children) from seven loaves and a few fish.

entries.author: The Blessed Bible Study Guide
entries.text:
**Peter's Confession and Jesus' Prediction of His Death**

**Themes:** Signs, Leaven of the Pharisees, Revelation of the Messiah, The Church, Suffering, Discipleship

**Outline:**
I. The Pharisees and Sadducees Demand a Sign (16:1-4)
II. The Leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees (16:5-12)
III. Peter Confesses Jesus as the Christ (16:13-20)
IV. Jesus Foretells His Death and Resurrection (16:21-23)
V. Take Up Your Cross and Follow Jesus (16:24-28)

**Summary:**
Jesus refuses a sign to the Pharisees and Sadducees, warning his disciples against their "leaven" (teaching). At Caesarea Philippi, Peter makes the foundational confession that Jesus is "the Christ, the Son of the living God." Jesus blesses Peter, promising to build his church. Immediately after, Jesus plainly predicts his impending suffering, death, and resurrection. When Peter objects, Jesus strongly rebukes him. Jesus then outlines the cost of discipleship: denying oneself, taking up one's cross, and following him.

entries.author: The Blessed Bible Study Guide
entries.text:
**The Transfiguration and the Healing of a Boy with a Demon**

**Themes:** Divine glory, The Law and Prophets, Faith, Passion prediction, Temple tax

**Outline:**
I. The Transfiguration (17:1-13)
II. Jesus Heals a Boy with a Demon (17:14-21)
III. Jesus Again Foretells Death, Resurrection (17:22-23)
IV. The Temple Tax (17:24-27)

**Summary:**
Jesus takes Peter, James, and John up a high mountain where he is transfigured in glory, appearing with Moses and Elijah. The Father's voice commands them to listen to his beloved Son. Descending, Jesus explains that "Elijah" has already come in the person of John the Baptist. He then heals a demon-possessed boy whom the disciples could not cure, attributing their failure to little faith. Jesus again predicts his death, and later miraculous provides a coin from a fish's mouth to pay the temple tax.

entries.author: The Blessed Bible Study Guide
entries.text:
**Discourse on the Church: Humility, Sin, and Forgiveness**

**Themes:** Humility, Care for little ones, Church discipline, Forgiveness, Grace

**Outline:**
I. Who Is the Greatest? (18:1-6)
II. Temptations to Sin (18:7-9)
III. The Parable of the Lost Sheep (18:10-14)
IV. If Your Brother Sins Against You (18:15-20)
V. The Parable of the Unforgiving Servant (18:21-35)

**Summary:**
In a discourse on relationships within the Kingdom, Jesus teaches that true greatness requires humility like that of a child, and severely warns against causing "little ones" to stumble. He illustrates God's care for every believer with the Parable of the Lost Sheep. He provides a procedure for addressing sin in the church (church discipline). Prompted by Peter's question on forgiveness, Jesus tells the Parable of the Unforgiving Servant, stressing that those forgiven immense debts by God must forgive others.

entries.author: The Blessed Bible Study Guide
entries.text:
**Teachings on Divorce, Children, and Wealth**

**Themes:** Marriage, Divorce, Celibacy, Childlike faith, Riches, Eternal life, Rewards

**Outline:**
I. Teaching About Divorce (19:1-12)
II. Let the Children Come to Me (19:13-15)
III. The Rich Young Man (19:16-30)

**Summary:**
Jesus travels to Judea where Pharisees test him on divorce. He affirms God's original design for lifelong marriage, allowing divorce only for sexual immorality, and discusses celibacy. He welcomes little children, laying hands on them and declaring the kingdom belongs to such as these. A rich young man asks how to get eternal life but walks away sorrowful when told to sell his possessions, prompting Jesus to teach on the danger of wealth and the promised rewards for his followers.

entries.author: The Blessed Bible Study Guide
entries.text:
**The Parable of the Laborers and the Journey to Jerusalem**

**Themes:** Grace, Equality of reward, Suffering, Servant leadership, Healing

**Outline:**
I. Laborers in the Vineyard (20:1-16)
II. Jesus Foretells His Death a Third Time (20:17-19)
III. A Mother's Request (20:20-28)
IV. Jesus Heals Two Blind Men (20:29-34)

**Summary:**
Jesus tells the Parable of the Laborers in the Vineyard, illustrating God's sovereign grace where the last shall be first and equal reward is given regardless of time served. Heading toward Jerusalem, Jesus predicts his crucifixion for a third time. The mother of James and John requests places of honor for her sons, prompting Jesus to teach that true greatness in his kingdom comes through serving and giving one's life as a ransom. Leaving Jericho, he heals two blind men who cry out for mercy.

entries.author: The Blessed Bible Study Guide
entries.text:
**The Triumphal Entry and Controversies in the Temple**

**Themes:** Messianic king, Cleansing the temple, Authority, Rejection, Judgment on Israel

**Outline:**
I. The Triumphal Entry (21:1-11)
II. Jesus Cleanses the Temple (21:12-17)
III. Jesus Curses the Fig Tree (21:18-22)
IV. The Authority of Jesus Challenged (21:23-27)
V. The Parable of the Two Sons (21:28-32)
VI. The Parable of the Tenants (21:33-46)

**Summary:**
Jesus enters Jerusalem riding on a donkey, fulfilling Zechariah's prophecy, while crowds praise him as the Son of David. He cleanses the temple, overturning the money changers' tables. The next day, he curses a barren fig tree as an object lesson on faith. In the temple, the religious leaders challenge his authority. Jesus responds with questions and parables—the Two Sons and the Tenants—that indict the leaders for rejecting God's messengers and eventually God's own Son, transferring the kingdom to others.

entries.author: The Blessed Bible Study Guide
entries.text:
**Parables, Traps, and the Greatest Commandment**

**Themes:** Kingdom invitation, Rejection, Taxes, Resurrection, The Greatest Commandment, David's Lord

**Outline:**
I. The Parable of the Wedding Feast (22:1-14)
II. Paying Taxes to Caesar (22:15-22)
III. Sadducees Ask About the Resurrection (22:23-33)
IV. The Great Commandment (22:34-40)
V. Whose Son Is the Christ? (22:41-46)

**Summary:**
Jesus tells the Parable of the Wedding Feast, illustrating the rejection of God's invitation by Israel's leaders and the inclusion of both good and bad, while warning against entering without the proper "wedding garment." The Pharisees and Herodians try to trap him regarding taxes to Caesar, but he answers wisely. The Sadducees question him about the resurrection, which he defends from Scripture. He summarizes the Law into loving God and loving neighbor. Finally, Jesus silences his critics by asking how David can call the Messiah "Lord."

entries.author: The Blessed Bible Study Guide
entries.text:
**Seven Woes to the Scribes and Pharisees**

**Themes:** Hypocrisy, Pride, False teaching, Judgment, Lament over Jerusalem

**Outline:**
I. A Warning Against Hypocrisy (23:1-12)
II. Seven Woes to the Scribes and Pharisees (23:13-36)
III. Lament over Jerusalem (23:37-39)

**Summary:**
Jesus addresses the crowds and disciples, warning them against the hypocrisy and pride of the scribes and Pharisees, who preach but do not practice, and seek honor for themselves. He pronounces seven severe "woes" upon the religious leaders, condemning them for hindering others from the kingdom, misplaced priorities, inner corruption while maintaining outward purity, and persecuting the prophets. He concludes with a heartbreaking lament over Jerusalem's impending desolation due to their rejection of him.

entries.author: The Blessed Bible Study Guide
entries.text:
**The Olivet Discourse: Signs of the End of the Age**

**Themes:** Destruction of the temple, Tribulation, Second Coming, Watchfulness, Judgment

**Outline:**
I. Jesus Foretells Destruction of the Temple (24:1-2)
II. Signs of the End of the Age (24:3-14)
III. The Abomination of Desolation (24:15-28)
IV. The Coming of the Son of Man (24:29-31)
V. The Lesson of the Fig Tree (24:32-35)
VI. No One Knows That Day and Hour (24:36-51)

**Summary:**
Leaving the temple, Jesus predicts its total destruction. On the Mount of Olives, the disciples ask about the signs of his coming and the end of the age. Jesus outlines a period of wars, famines, and intense persecution, referring to the "abomination of desolation." He describes his glorious, visible return (the coming of the Son of Man) to gather the elect. Because the exact time is unknown, he stresses the absolute necessity for his followers to remain watchful, ready, and faithful.

entries.author: The Blessed Bible Study Guide
entries.text:
**The Olivet Discourse: Parables of Readiness and the Final Judgment**

**Themes:** Preparation, Stewardship, Final Judgment, Sheep and goats, Eternal destiny

**Outline:**
I. The Parable of the Ten Virgins (25:1-13)
II. The Parable of the Talents (25:14-30)
III. The Final Judgment (25:31-46)

**Summary:**
Jesus continues the Olivet Discourse with parables emphasizing readiness. The Parable of the Ten Virgins contrasts wise preparation with foolish negligence. The Parable of the Talents teaches that believers must faithfully steward what God has entrusted to them until he returns. Finally, Jesus depicts the final judgment, where the Son of Man will separate the nations like sheep and goats, based on how they treated "the least of these" his brothers, resulting in eternal punishment or eternal life.

entries.author: The Blessed Bible Study Guide
entries.text:
**The Plot, The Last Supper, Gethsemane, and the Arrest**

**Themes:** Betrayal, Passover, New Covenant, Agony, Submission to the Father's will, Arrest, Trial

**Outline:**
I. The Plot to Kill Jesus and the Anointing at Bethany (26:1-13)
II. Judas to Betray Jesus (26:14-16)
III. The Passover and the Lord's Supper (26:17-29)
IV. Jesus Foretells Peter's Denial (26:30-35)
V. Jesus Prays in Gethsemane (26:36-46)
VI. Betrayal and Arrest of Jesus (26:47-56)
VII. Jesus Before Caiaphas and the Council (26:57-68)
VIII. Peter Denies Jesus (26:69-75)

**Summary:**
As the leaders plot his death, a woman anoints Jesus in Bethany, an act he defends as preparation for burial. Judas agrees to betray Jesus for thirty pieces of silver. Jesus eats the Passover meal with his disciples, instituting the Lord's Supper. He predicts Peter's denial. In Gethsemane, Jesus agonizes in prayer, submitting to the Father's will. Judas arrives with an armed crowd to arrest him. Jesus is tried before the high priest Caiaphas, mocked, and beaten, while outside in the courtyard, Peter denies him three times.

entries.author: The Blessed Bible Study Guide
entries.text:
**The Trial, Crucifixion, and Burial of Jesus**

**Themes:** Innocence, Atonement, Substitution, Suffering, Death, Burial

**Outline:**
I. Jesus Delivered to Pilate and the Death of Judas (27:1-10)
II. Jesus Before Pilate (27:11-26)
III. Jesus Is Mocked (27:27-31)
IV. The Crucifixion (27:32-44)
V. The Death of Jesus (27:45-56)
VI. Jesus Is Buried (27:57-61)
VII. The Guard at the Tomb (27:62-66)

**Summary:**
Jesus is handed over to Pilate. Judas, filled with remorse, hangs himself. Despite recognizing Jesus' innocence, Pilate bows to the crowd's demand to release Barabbas and crucify Jesus. Soldiers brutally mock and scourge Jesus before leading him to Golgotha. Jesus is crucified between two robbers. Darkness covers the land, and Jesus dies, accompanied by an earthquake and the tearing of the temple curtain. Joseph of Arimathea buries him in a new tomb, which the religious leaders secure with a seal and a Roman guard.

entries.author: The Blessed Bible Study Guide
entries.text:
**The Resurrection and the Great Commission**

**Themes:** Resurrection, Victory over death, Deception, Authority, The Great Commission

**Outline:**
I. The Resurrection (28:1-10)
II. The Report of the Guard (28:11-15)
III. The Great Commission (28:16-20)

**Summary:**
On Sunday morning, Mary Magdalene and the other Mary find the tomb empty; an angel rolls away the stone and announces that Jesus is risen. Jesus appears to the women, instructing them to tell the brothers to go to Galilee. Meanwhile, the religious leaders bribe the guards to lie and say the disciples stole the body. In Galilee, the resurrected Jesus appears to the eleven disciples, claiming all authority and commissioning them to make disciples of all nations, promising his presence to the end of the age.

entries.author: The Blessed Bible Study Guide
entries.text:
**Thanksgiving for the Thessalonians' Faith**

**Themes:** Faith, Hope, Love, Election, Example

**Outline:**
1. Greeting (1:1)
2. Thanksgiving for their faith and love (1:2-3)
3. Assurance of their election and reception of the Gospel (1:4-7)
4. The spread of their faith as an example (1:8-10)

**Summary:**
Paul opens his letter by expressing deep gratitude for the Thessalonians' active faith, labor of love, and steadfast hope. He reminds them of how they warmly received the gospel with the Holy Spirit's power and became exemplary models to all believers in Macedonia and Achaia by turning from idols to serve the living God.

entries.author: The Blessed Bible Study Guide
entries.text:
**Paul's Ministry in Thessalonica**

**Themes:** Sincere Ministry, Suffering, Parental Care, God's Word

**Outline:**
1. The purity of Paul's motives and ministry (2:1-6)
2. Paul's gentle, parental care for the church (2:7-12)
3. The Thessalonians' reception of God's Word amid suffering (2:13-16)
4. Paul's longing to see them (2:17-20)

**Summary:**
Paul defends the integrity of his ministry among the Thessalonians, emphasizing his gentle, nurturing care for them like a nursing mother and an encouraging father. He praises them for accepting his message as the true word of God and enduring persecution, expressing his intense desire to visit them again despite Satan's hindrances.

entries.author: The Blessed Bible Study Guide
entries.text:
**Timothy's Encouraging Report**

**Themes:** Concern, Encouragement, Faith in Affliction, Prayer

**Outline:**
1. Sending Timothy to strengthen their faith (3:1-5)
2. Timothy's good report about their faith and love (3:6-8)
3. Paul's thanksgiving and prayer for them (3:9-13)

**Summary:**
Unable to bear his anxiety any longer, Paul explains that he sent Timothy to check on their faith amidst their afflictions. He rejoices over Timothy's encouraging report of their strong faith and affection, and he prays earnestly that God will clear the way for him to visit them and that their hearts may be strengthened in holiness.

entries.author: The Blessed Bible Study Guide
entries.text:
**Living to Please God and the Coming of the Lord**

**Themes:** Sanctification, Sexual Purity, Brotherly Love, The Rapture, Hope

**Outline:**
1. Exhortation to sexual purity and holiness (4:1-8)
2. Encouragement to love one another and live quietly (4:9-12)
3. The hope of the resurrection and the Lord's return (4:13-18)

**Summary:**
Paul instructs the believers on how to live lives pleasing to God, emphasizing sexual purity, sanctification, and growing in brotherly love. He also addresses their concerns about believers who have died, assuring them that at the Lord's return, the dead in Christ will rise first, and then the living will be caught up together with them, offering profound comfort.

entries.author: The Blessed Bible Study Guide
entries.text:
**The Day of the Lord and Final Exhortations**

**Themes:** Vigilance, The Day of the Lord, Christian Conduct, Sanctification

**Outline:**
1. Readiness for the Day of the Lord (5:1-11)
2. Instructions for congregational life and leadership (5:12-15)
3. Final exhortations and prayer for sanctification (5:16-28)

**Summary:**
Discussing the sudden and unexpected nature of the 'Day of the Lord,' Paul urges the Thessalonians to stay awake and sober, armed with faith, love, and hope. He concludes the letter with rapid-fire instructions on honoring leaders, rejoicing always, praying continually, holding fast to what is good, and a final prayer for their complete sanctification.

entries.author: The Blessed Bible Study Guide
entries.text:
**Thanksgiving and Comfort in Persecution**

**Themes:** Perseverance, God's Righteous Judgment, Glorification

**Outline:**
1. Greeting (1:1-2)
2. Thanksgiving for their growing faith and endurance (1:3-4)
3. The righteous judgment of God at Christ's return (1:5-10)
4. Prayer for their calling and glorification (1:11-12)

**Summary:**
Paul begins his second letter by praising the Thessalonians for their flourishing faith and steadfast endurance through ongoing persecutions. He comforts them with the promise that God will execute perfect justice when Jesus is revealed from heaven, punishing their afflictors and being glorified in His saints.

entries.author: The Blessed Bible Study Guide
entries.text:
**The Man of Lawlessness**

**Themes:** The Day of the Lord, Antichrist, Deception, Standing Firm

**Outline:**
1. Correction regarding the Day of the Lord (2:1-2)
2. The rebellion and the man of lawlessness (2:3-12)
3. Thanksgiving for their salvation and call to stand firm (2:13-17)

**Summary:**
Addressing a false rumor that the Day of the Lord had already come, Paul clarifies that it will not occur until the rebellion happens and the 'man of lawlessness' is revealed. He warns of the great deception that will accompany this figure but encourages the believers to stand firm in the teachings they received, thanking God for their salvation.

entries.author: The Blessed Bible Study Guide
entries.text:
**Exhortation to Work and Final Greetings**

**Themes:** Prayer, Diligence, Discipline, Peace

**Outline:**
1. Request for prayer for the spread of the Gospel (3:1-5)
2. Warning against idleness and indiscipline (3:6-15)
3. Final blessing and greeting (3:16-18)

**Summary:**
Paul asks for prayers for the rapid spread of the gospel and protection from evil people. He then strongly commands the believers to avoid idleness, using his own hard-working example to instruct that those who refuse to work should not eat, and concludes with a prayer for peace and his personal greeting.

entries.author: The Blessed Bible Study Guide
entries.text:
**Warning Against False Teachers and Grace to Paul**

**Themes:** False Doctrine, The Law, Grace, Mercy, A Good Conscience

**Outline:**
1. Greeting (1:1-2)
2. Warning against false teachers and misuse of the law (1:3-11)
3. The Lord's superabundant grace to Paul (1:12-17)
4. Charge to Timothy to fight the good fight (1:18-20)

**Summary:**
Paul charges Timothy to stay in Ephesus to command certain men not to teach false doctrines or devote themselves to myths and endless genealogies. He reflects on his own past as a blasphemer and persecutor, marveling at the immense grace and mercy of Christ Jesus, and urges Timothy to hold on to faith and a good conscience.

entries.author: The Blessed Bible Study Guide
entries.text:
**Instructions on Worship**

**Themes:** Prayer for All, Mediation of Christ, Roles in Worship, Modesty

**Outline:**
1. The necessity of prayer for all people and leaders (2:1-7)
2. Instructions for men and women in worship (2:8-15)

**Summary:**
Paul instructs that prayers, intercessions, and thanksgivings be made for all people, especially kings and those in authority, highlighting that there is one God and one mediator, Jesus Christ. He provides specific instructions for public worship, calling men to pray without anger and women to dress modestly and learn in quiet submission.

entries.author: The Blessed Bible Study Guide
entries.text:
**Qualifications for Overseers and Deacons**

**Themes:** Church Leadership, Character, Mystery of Godliness

**Outline:**
1. Qualifications for overseers/elders (3:1-7)
2. Qualifications for deacons and their wives (3:8-13)
3. The mystery of godliness in the church (3:14-16)

**Summary:**
Paul outlines the strict moral, spiritual, and relational qualifications required for church leaders, including overseers and deacons, emphasizing blameless character, self-control, and good management of their own families. He explains that he writes these things so people know how to conduct themselves in the church, which upholds the profound mystery of godliness.

entries.author: The Blessed Bible Study Guide
entries.text:
**Instructions to Timothy about False Teaching**

**Themes:** Apostasy, Asceticism, Godliness, Pastoral Duties

**Outline:**
1. The Spirit's warning of later apostasy and false teaching (4:1-5)
2. Being a good servant of Christ Jesus (4:6-10)
3. Instructions for Timothy's personal life and ministry (4:11-16)

**Summary:**
Paul warns that in later times some will abandon the faith, following deceiving spirits and hypocritical liars who forbid marriage and certain foods. He instructs Timothy to counter this by nourishing himself on the truths of the faith, training himself in godliness, and being an example in speech, conduct, love, faith, and purity.

entries.author: The Blessed Bible Study Guide
entries.text:
**Instructions for Widows, Elders, and Slaves**

**Themes:** Honor, Care for Widows, Church Discipline, Fairness

**Outline:**
1. Guidelines for interacting with different age groups (5:1-2)
2. Caring for true widows and family responsibilities (5:3-16)
3. Honoring, disciplining, and selecting elders (5:17-25)

**Summary:**
Paul provides practical guidelines for pastoral care, detailing how to respectfully treat older and younger men and women. He lays out comprehensive rules for the church's support of truly destitute widows, the financial support and discipline of elders, and cautions Timothy to avoid partiality and hasty ordinations.

entries.author: The Blessed Bible Study Guide
entries.text:
**False Teachers and the Love of Money**

**Themes:** Contentment, Wealth, False Teaching, The Good Fight of Faith

**Outline:**
1. Instructions for slaves (6:1-2)
2. The danger of false teaching and the love of money (6:3-10)
3. Charge to Timothy to pursue godliness (6:11-16)
4. Instructions for the rich and final charge (6:17-21)

**Summary:**
After addressing believing slaves, Paul condemns false teachers who treat godliness as a means to financial gain, famously warning that the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil. He charges Timothy to flee these desires, pursue righteousness, fight the good faith, and instruct the wealthy to be generous and rich in good deeds.

entries.author: The Blessed Bible Study Guide
entries.text:
**Thanksgiving and Call to Faithfulness**

**Themes:** Sincere Faith, Courage, Suffering for the Gospel, Guarding the Truth

**Outline:**
1. Greeting and thanksgiving for Timothy's faith (1:1-5)
2. Appeal to fan the flame of God's gift and not be ashamed (1:6-12)
3. Exhortation to guard the good deposit (1:13-18)

**Summary:**
Paul, writing from prison, warmly recalls Timothy's sincere faith and heritage, urging him to fan into flame the spiritual gift he received. He exhorts Timothy not to be ashamed of the gospel or of Paul the prisoner, but to join in suffering for the truth and to fiercely guard the good deposit of sound teaching.

entries.author: The Blessed Bible Study Guide
entries.text:
**A Good Soldier of Christ Jesus**

**Themes:** Endurance, Discipleship, Diligence, Purity, Avoiding Quarrels

**Outline:**
1. Entrusting the gospel to reliable people (2:1-2)
2. Metaphors of endurance: soldier, athlete, farmer (2:3-13)
3. A worker approved by God, avoiding foolish controversies (2:14-26)

**Summary:**
Paul encourages Timothy to be strong in grace and to pass on his teachings to reliable people. Using the metaphors of a dedicated soldier, a rule-following athlete, and a hardworking farmer, Paul emphasizes the necessity of endurance and suffering for Christ, instructing Timothy to correctly handle the word of truth and flee youthful passions.

entries.author: The Blessed Bible Study Guide
entries.text:
**Godlessness in the Last Days**

**Themes:** Moral Decay, Persecution, Scripture, Equipping

**Outline:**
1. Terrible times and godlessness in the last days (3:1-9)
2. Paul's example of suffering and endurance (3:10-13)
3. The inspiration and usefulness of Scripture (3:14-17)

**Summary:**
Paul warns of terrible times in the last days characterized by extreme moral decay and people having a form of godliness but denying its power. He reminds Timothy of the persecutions Paul himself has endured and charges him to stand firm in the sacred Scriptures, which are God-breathed and completely sufficient to equip the believer for every good work.

entries.author: The Blessed Bible Study Guide
entries.text:
**Final Charge to Timothy**

**Themes:** Preach the Word, Finishing the Race, Loneliness, God's Faithfulness

**Outline:**
1. Solemn charge to preach the Word (4:1-5)
2. Paul's valedictory: finishing the race (4:6-8)
3. Personal requests, updates, and final greetings (4:9-22)

**Summary:**
In his final words before his impending martyrdom, Paul gives a solemn charge to Timothy to preach the word in and out of season. Paul reflects on his life, declaring that he has fought the good fight and kept the faith, and concludes with personal requests for his cloak and scrolls, expressing trust in the Lord's deliverance into His heavenly kingdom.

entries.author: The Blessed Bible Study Guide
entries.text:
**Qualifications for Elders and Rebuking False Teachers**

**Themes:** Church Order, Leadership Qualifications, Rebuking Error

**Outline:**
1. Greeting and purpose of the letter (1:1-4)
2. Appointing qualified elders in Crete (1:5-9)
3. Correcting rebellious false teachers (1:10-16)

**Summary:**
Paul writes to Titus, whom he left in Crete to put the church in order and appoint elders in every town. He lists the rigorous moral and doctrinal qualifications for these leaders and stresses the urgent need to silence rebellious false teachers, especially those of the circumcision group, who are ruining entire households for dishonest gain.

entries.author: The Blessed Bible Study Guide
entries.text:
**Teaching Sound Doctrine**

**Themes:** Sound Doctrine, Christian Conduct, Grace, Blessed Hope

**Outline:**
1. Instructions for different groups in the church (2:1-10)
2. The grace of God and the blessed hope (2:11-15)

**Summary:**
Paul instructs Titus to teach what accords with sound doctrine, outlining specific behaviors expected of older men, older women, younger women, younger men, and slaves. He roots these ethical commands in the grace of God, which brings salvation, trains believers to renounce ungodliness, and points them toward the blessed hope of Christ's glorious return.

entries.author: The Blessed Bible Study Guide
entries.text:
**Doing What is Good**

**Themes:** Submission, Salvation by Mercy, Good Works, Avoiding Divisiveness

**Outline:**
1. Christian conduct in society and the basis of salvation (3:1-8)
2. Avoiding foolish controversies and divisive people (3:9-11)
3. Final remarks and greetings (3:12-15)

**Summary:**
Paul reminds the believers to be submissive to rulers, peaceable, and considerate, recalling that they were once foolish but were saved entirely by God's mercy and the washing of regeneration. He urges them to devote themselves to doing good works while strictly avoiding foolish controversies and warning divisive individuals.

entries.author: The Blessed Bible Study Guide
entries.text:
**Plea for Onesimus**

**Themes:** Forgiveness, Reconciliation, Brotherhood in Christ, Grace

**Outline:**
1. Greeting and thanksgiving for Philemon's love and faith (1:1-7)
2. Paul's appeal for Onesimus (1:8-16)
3. Paul's pledge to repay Onesimus' debts (1:17-22)
4. Final greetings (1:23-25)

**Summary:**
In this deeply personal letter, Paul writes to Philemon, a wealthy Christian, on behalf of his runaway slave Onesimus, who has become a believer under Paul's ministry. Rather than commanding Philemon, Paul tactfully appeals to his love, asking him to welcome Onesimus back not as a slave but as a beloved brother in Christ, even offering to personally pay any debts Onesimus owes.

entries.author: The Blessed Bible Study Guide
entries.text:
**The Word Made Flesh**

**Themes:** Deity of Christ, Light vs. Darkness, Witness of John the Baptist, Calling of the First Disciples

**Outline:**
I. The Prologue (1:1-18)
II. John the Baptist's Testimony (1:19-34)
III. The First Disciples (1:35-51)

**Summary:**
John begins with a profound prologue identifying Jesus as the eternal Word (Logos) who became flesh. John the Baptist testifies that Jesus is the Lamb of God. Jesus begins calling his first disciples, including Andrew, Peter, Philip, and Nathanael.

entries.author: The Blessed Bible Study Guide
entries.text:
**The First Sign and the Temple Cleansing**

**Themes:** Miracles (Signs) as Revelation of Glory, New Covenant replacing the Old, Zeal for God's House

**Outline:**
I. The Wedding at Cana (2:1-12)
II. Cleansing the Temple (2:13-25)

**Summary:**
Jesus performs his first public miracle, turning water into wine at a wedding in Cana, symbolizing the joy and abundance of the new covenant. He then goes to Jerusalem and drives the merchants out of the temple, prophesying about his resurrection.

entries.author: The Blessed Bible Study Guide
entries.text:
**The New Birth**

**Themes:** Regeneration (Born Again), God's Love for the World, Spiritual vs. Fleshly Birth, John the Baptist's Humility

**Outline:**
I. Jesus and Nicodemus (3:1-21)
II. John the Baptist's Final Testimony (3:22-36)

**Summary:**
Nicodemus, a Pharisee, visits Jesus at night. Jesus teaches him that one must be 'born again' (or 'born from above') to see the kingdom of God. This chapter contains the famous verse John 3:16. John the Baptist rejoices at Jesus' growing ministry, saying 'He must increase, but I must decrease.'

entries.author: The Blessed Bible Study Guide
entries.text:
**The Woman at the Well**

**Themes:** Living Water, True Worship, Breaking Social/Racial Barriers, The Harvest

**Outline:**
I. Jesus and the Samaritan Woman (4:1-26)
II. The Disciples and the Harvest (4:27-38)
III. The Samaritans Believe (4:39-42)
IV. Healing the Official's Son (4:43-54)

**Summary:**
Jesus travels through Samaria and speaks with a Samaritan woman at Jacob's well, offering her 'living water.' She believes he is the Messiah and brings her village to him. Back in Galilee, Jesus performs his second sign by healing an official's son from a distance.

entries.author: The Blessed Bible Study Guide
entries.text:
**Healing at the Pool of Bethesda**

**Themes:** Sabbath Controversy, Equality with the Father, Life and Judgment, Witnesses to Christ

**Outline:**
I. The Healing at the Pool (5:1-15)
II. Jesus Claims Equality with God (5:16-30)
III. Testimonies about Jesus (5:31-47)

**Summary:**
Jesus heals a man who had been invalid for 38 years on the Sabbath. This leads to persecution by Jewish leaders. Jesus responds by claiming a unique relationship with God the Father, asserting his authority to give life and judge, and citing multiple witnesses to his identity.

entries.author: The Blessed Bible Study Guide
entries.text:
**The Bread of Life**

**Themes:** Jesus as the Bread of Life, Spiritual vs. Physical Food, Sovereignty in Salvation, Defection of Disciples

**Outline:**
I. Feeding the Five Thousand (6:1-15)
II. Jesus Walks on Water (6:16-21)
III. The Bread of Life Discourse (6:22-59)
IV. Reactions to the Teaching (6:60-71)

**Summary:**
After multiplying loaves and fishes and walking on water, Jesus delivers a difficult discourse, claiming he is the 'bread of life' and that one must eat his flesh and drink his blood. Many followers find this teaching too hard and leave him, but Peter confesses Jesus has the 'words of eternal life.'

entries.author: The Blessed Bible Study Guide
entries.text:
**The Feast of Booths**

**Themes:** Division over Jesus, Living Water, Divine Timing (Jesus' 'Hour'), Unbelief of Brothers

**Outline:**
I. Jesus goes Secretly to the Feast (7:1-13)
II. Jesus Teaches in the Temple (7:14-36)
III. Promise of the Holy Spirit (7:37-39)
IV. Division Among the People (7:40-53)

**Summary:**
Despite threats to his life, Jesus attends the Feast of Booths in Jerusalem. He teaches openly, causing widespread debate about whether he is the Prophet or the Christ. On the last day of the feast, he cries out offering the Holy Spirit as rivers of living water to those who believe.

entries.author: The Blessed Bible Study Guide
entries.text:
**The Light of the World**

**Themes:** Jesus as the Light, Spiritual Fatherhood (God vs. Satan), Truth and Freedom, The 'I Am' Statement

**Outline:**
I. The Woman Caught in Adultery (8:1-11)
II. Jesus the Light of the World (8:12-30)
III. True Disciples and True Children of Abraham (8:31-47)
IV. Jesus' Pre-existence (8:48-59)

**Summary:**
After dealing mercifully with a woman caught in adultery, Jesus declares 'I am the light of the world.' A fierce debate with Jewish leaders ensues regarding spiritual lineage. Jesus tells them the truth will set them free and dramatically claims eternal existence before Abraham ('I am').

entries.author: The Blessed Bible Study Guide
entries.text:
**Healing of the Man Born Blind**

**Themes:** Spiritual Blindness vs. Sight, The Problem of Suffering, Cost of Discipleship

**Outline:**
I. The Healing (9:1-12)
II. Investigation by the Pharisees (9:13-34)
III. Spiritual Blindness (9:35-41)

**Summary:**
Jesus heals a man born blind, stating that his blindness was for God's works to be displayed. The Pharisees launch a hostile investigation and ultimately excommunicate the healed man. Jesus reveals himself as the Son of Man to the outcast, while declaring the Pharisees to be spiritually blind.

entries.author: The Blessed Bible Study Guide
entries.text:
**The Good Shepherd**

**Themes:** Jesus as the Shepherd and the Door, Intimacy with the Flock, Security of the Believer, Deity of Christ

**Outline:**
I. The Good Shepherd Discourse (10:1-21)
II. Conflict at the Feast of Dedication (10:22-42)

**Summary:**
Jesus describes himself as the Good Shepherd who lays down his life for his sheep, contrasting himself with thieves and hired hands. Later, at the Feast of Dedication, he states plainly 'I and the Father are one,' prompting the religious leaders to attempt to stone him for blasphemy.

entries.author: The Blessed Bible Study Guide
entries.text:
**The Resurrection of Lazarus**

**Themes:** Resurrection and Life, Jesus' Power over Death, Divine Timing, The Final Catalyst for the Plot against Jesus

**Outline:**
I. The Death of Lazarus (11:1-16)
II. Jesus the Resurrection and the Life (11:17-37)
III. Raising Lazarus (11:38-44)
IV. The Plot to Kill Jesus (11:45-57)

**Summary:**
Lazarus, a dear friend of Jesus, falls ill and dies. Jesus delays his arrival, later proclaiming to Martha, 'I am the resurrection and the life.' He raises Lazarus from the tomb after four days. This stunning miracle becomes the tipping point for the Sanhedrin, who officially plot to kill him.

entries.author: The Blessed Bible Study Guide
entries.text:
**The Triumphal Entry and the Coming Hour**

**Themes:** Devotion to Christ, Prophetic Fulfillment, The Grain of Wheat, The Judgment of the World

**Outline:**
I. Mary Anoints Jesus (12:1-11)
II. The Triumphal Entry (12:12-19)
III. Jesus Predicts His Death (12:20-36)
IV. The Unbelief of the People (12:37-50)

**Summary:**
Mary anoints Jesus with expensive ointment at Bethany. Jesus enters Jerusalem to adoring crowds. When some Greeks seek him, Jesus declares his 'hour' has come, using the metaphor of a dying seed producing much fruit. Despite his signs, many refuse to believe, fulfilling Isaiah's prophecies.

entries.author: The Blessed Bible Study Guide
entries.text:
**Washing the Disciples' Feet**

**Themes:** Servant Leadership, Love for One Another, Betrayal, The Upper Room Discourse begins

**Outline:**
I. Jesus Washes His Disciples' Feet (13:1-20)
II. Jesus Predicts His Betrayal (13:21-30)
III. The New Commandment (13:31-35)
IV. Jesus Predicts Peter's Denial (13:36-38)

**Summary:**
During the Last Supper, Jesus models ultimate humility by washing his disciples' feet. He predicts that Judas will betray him and that Peter will deny him. He gives his followers a new commandment: to love one another just as he has loved them.

entries.author: The Blessed Bible Study Guide
entries.text:
**The Way, the Truth, and the Life**

**Themes:** Comfort in Christ, Jesus as the Only Way, The Promise of the Holy Spirit (Paraclete), Peace

**Outline:**
I. Jesus the Way to the Father (14:1-14)
II. The Promise of the Holy Spirit (14:15-31)

**Summary:**
Jesus comforts his troubled disciples, promising to prepare a place for them and declaring himself 'the way, and the truth, and the life.' He promises to send the Holy Spirit, the Helper, who will dwell within them, and he leaves them with his supernatural peace.

entries.author: The Blessed Bible Study Guide
entries.text:
**The True Vine**

**Themes:** Abiding in Christ, Fruitfulness, The World's Hatred, Friendship with Jesus

**Outline:**
I. The Vine and the Branches (15:1-17)
II. The Hatred of the World (15:18-27)

**Summary:**
Using the metaphor of the vine and the branches, Jesus emphasizes the absolute necessity of abiding in him to produce spiritual fruit. He calls his disciples 'friends.' He also warns them that just as the world hated him, it will hate them, but the Spirit will bear witness.

entries.author: The Blessed Bible Study Guide
entries.text:
**The Work of the Holy Spirit**

**Themes:** The Ministry of the Spirit, Overcoming the World, Grief Turning to Joy, Prayer in Jesus' Name

**Outline:**
I. The Work of the Holy Spirit (16:1-15)
II. Sorrow will Turn into Joy (16:16-24)
III. Jesus has Overcome the World (16:25-33)

**Summary:**
Jesus explains that it is to their advantage that he leaves, so the Helper will come. The Spirit will convict the world of sin, righteousness, and judgment. Jesus assures them that their coming sorrow will turn to profound joy, concluding with the victory cry: 'I have overcome the world.'

entries.author: The Blessed Bible Study Guide
entries.text:
**The High Priestly Prayer**

**Themes:** Glory, Unity, Sanctification in Truth, Jesus' Intercession for Believers

**Outline:**
I. Jesus Prays for Himself (17:1-5)
II. Jesus Prays for His Disciples (17:6-19)
III. Jesus Prays for All Future Believers (17:20-26)

**Summary:**
In his longest recorded prayer, Jesus asks the Father to glorify him. He prays for the protection and sanctification of his disciples. He then extends his prayer to all who will ever believe in him through their message, praying passionately for their unity so the world may believe.

entries.author: The Blessed Bible Study Guide
entries.text:
**Betrayal, Arrest, and Trial**

**Themes:** Jesus' Sovereign Control, Two Kingdoms, Truth, Fulfilling the Father's Cup

**Outline:**
I. Betrayal and Arrest (18:1-11)
II. Jesus Before Annas and Peter's Denials (18:12-27)
III. Jesus Before Pilate (18:28-40)

**Summary:**
Judas leads soldiers to the garden, where Jesus willingly surrenders, asserting his 'I am' identity. Peter denies knowing Jesus. Jesus is taken before Annas and Caiaphas, and then to Pilate, where he declares that his kingdom is not of this world and that he came to bear witness to the truth.

entries.author: The Blessed Bible Study Guide
entries.text:
**Crucifixion and Burial**

**Themes:** Substitutionary Atonement, Fulfillment of Scripture, The Finished Work of Christ

**Outline:**
I. Jesus is Scourged and Condemned (19:1-16)
II. The Crucifixion (19:17-27)
III. The Death of Jesus (19:28-37)
IV. The Burial (19:38-42)

**Summary:**
Pilate gives in to the crowd and sentences Jesus to death. Jesus is crucified at Golgotha. After ensuring his mother is cared for by John, he drinks the sour wine and cries out, 'It is finished.' Joseph of Arimathea and Nicodemus respectfully bury his body in a new tomb.

entries.author: The Blessed Bible Study Guide
entries.text:
**The Resurrection**

**Themes:** Triumph over Death, Believing without Seeing, Commissioning the Disciples, The Purpose of the Gospel

**Outline:**
I. The Empty Tomb (20:1-10)
II. Jesus Appears to Mary Magdalene (20:11-18)
III. Jesus Appears to the Disciples (20:19-23)
IV. Jesus and Thomas (20:24-29)
V. The Purpose of the Book (20:30-31)

**Summary:**
Mary Magdalene finds the tomb empty. Jesus appears first to her, then to the disciples behind locked doors, breathing the Holy Spirit on them. A week later, he appears to 'Doubting Thomas,' who confesses him as 'My Lord and my God!' John explicitly states the Gospel was written so readers may believe and have life.

entries.author: The Blessed Bible Study Guide
entries.text:
**Epilogue: Restoration and Commission**

**Themes:** Restoration of the Fallen, Feeding the Flock, Following Christ without Comparison

**Outline:**
I. The Miraculous Catch of Fish (21:1-14)
II. Jesus Restores Peter (21:15-19)
III. The Beloved Disciple and Conclusion (21:20-25)

**Summary:**
In a post-resurrection appearance by the Sea of Galilee, Jesus provides a miraculous catch of fish. He gently restores Peter, who had denied him three times, by asking him three times if he loves him, instructing him to 'feed my sheep.' The Gospel ends affirming the truthfulness of the disciple's testimony.

entries.author: The Blessed Bible Study Guide
entries.text:
**Comfort in Affliction**

**Themes:** Comfort, Suffering, Sincerity, Reliability of God

**Outline:**
I. Salutation (1:1-2)
II. The God of All Comfort (1:3-11)
III. Paul's Change of Plans (1:12-24)

**Summary:**
Paul opens his letter by praising God as the source of all comfort, who comforts believers in their afflictions so they can comfort others. He explains his recent severe suffering in Asia. He then defends his integrity and sincerity, clarifying why he had to alter his travel plans to visit Corinth, assuring them that God's promises in Christ are always 'Yes.'

entries.author: The Blessed Bible Study Guide
entries.text:
**Forgiveness and the Aroma of Christ**

**Themes:** Forgiveness, Restoration, Triumph in Christ

**Outline:**
I. A Painful Visit Avoided (2:1-4)
II. Forgiveness for the Offender (2:5-11)
III. Ministry in Troas and Macedonia (2:12-13)
IV. Triumphant Ministry (2:14-17)

**Summary:**
Paul explains he wrote his previous 'severe letter' out of deep love, not to cause pain. He urges the Corinthians to forgive and comfort the person who had caused grief, lest Satan outwit them. Paul describes his anxiety waiting for Titus and rejoices that God always leads believers in triumph in Christ, making them the pleasing aroma of Christ to God.

entries.author: The Blessed Bible Study Guide
entries.text:
**Ministers of the New Covenant**

**Themes:** New Covenant, The Spirit vs. The Letter, Glory of the Gospel

**Outline:**
I. Letters of Recommendation (3:1-3)
II. The Glory of the New Covenant (3:4-11)
III. The Veil Removed (3:12-18)

**Summary:**
Paul asserts that he doesn't need letters of recommendation because the Corinthians themselves are his letter, written by the Spirit on human hearts. He contrasts the glory of the old covenant of the law, which is fading, with the surpassing glory of the new covenant of the Spirit. With unveiled faces, believers are transformed into the Lord's image.

entries.author: The Blessed Bible Study Guide
entries.text:
**Treasure in Jars of Clay**

**Themes:** Perseverance, Light of the Gospel, Earthly Frailty, Eternal Glory

**Outline:**
I. The Light of the Gospel (4:1-6)
II. Treasure in Jars of Clay (4:7-12)
III. Living by Faith (4:13-18)

**Summary:**
Paul proclaims the light of the gospel, noting that Satan has blinded the minds of unbelievers. He describes believers as fragile 'jars of clay' holding the treasure of the gospel, showing that this all-surpassing power is from God. Despite facing severe hardships, Paul doesn't lose heart, knowing that temporary troubles achieve an eternal glory.

entries.author: The Blessed Bible Study Guide
entries.text:
**The Ministry of Reconciliation**

**Themes:** Heavenly Dwelling, Judgment, New Creation, Reconciliation

**Outline:**
I. Our Heavenly Dwelling (5:1-10)
II. The Ministry of Reconciliation (5:11-21)

**Summary:**
Paul anticipates the eternal, heavenly body that awaits believers, groaning for this heavenly dwelling. He reminds them of the judgment seat of Christ. He explains that knowing the fear of the Lord drives his ministry, declaring that anyone in Christ is a new creation. God has given believers the ministry of reconciliation, calling them to be Christ's ambassadors.

entries.author: The Blessed Bible Study Guide
entries.text:
**Hardships and Purity**

**Themes:** Endurance in Ministry, Unequal Yokes, Holiness

**Outline:**
I. Paul's Hardships in Ministry (6:1-13)
II. Warning Against Yoking with Unbelievers (6:14-18)

**Summary:**
Paul describes the intense hardships and trials he and his companions have endured as servants of God, pleading with the Corinthians to open their hearts wide. He follows this with a strong exhortation not to be unequally yoked with unbelievers, urging them to separate from impurity so that God may dwell among them.

entries.author: The Blessed Bible Study Guide
entries.text:
**Joy in Repentance**

**Themes:** Godly Sorrow, Repentance, Comfort, Joy

**Outline:**
I. Exhortation to Holiness (7:1)
II. Paul's Joy over the Corinthians' Repentance (7:2-16)

**Summary:**
Concluding his plea for purity, Paul asks the Corinthians to make room for him in their hearts. He expresses his profound joy at the arrival of Titus, who brought news of their longing, deep sorrow, and zeal for Paul. He contrasts godly sorrow, which brings repentance and salvation, with worldly sorrow, celebrating their renewed relationship.

entries.author: The Blessed Bible Study Guide
entries.text:
**The Grace of Giving**

**Themes:** Generosity, Collection for the Saints, Equality

**Outline:**
I. The Generosity of the Macedonians (8:1-7)
II. Christ's Example of Grace (8:8-15)
III. Titus Sent to Receive the Collection (8:16-24)

**Summary:**
Paul urges the Corinthians to excel in the grace of giving, citing the extreme generosity of the Macedonian churches despite their poverty. He points to the example of Christ, who became poor so that others might become rich. Paul commends Titus and other brothers who are coming to Corinth to help administer the collection for the saints.

entries.author: The Blessed Bible Study Guide
entries.text:
**God Loves a Cheerful Giver**

**Themes:** Sowing and Reaping, Cheerful Giving, Thanksgiving

**Outline:**
I. Readiness to Give (9:1-5)
II. Bountiful Sowing and Reaping (9:6-15)

**Summary:**
Paul continues his discussion on the collection for the saints in Jerusalem, praising the Corinthians' initial eagerness. He uses the principle of sowing and reaping to encourage them to give generously and cheerfully, not under compulsion. He assures them that God will abundantly provide for them and that their generosity will result in thanksgiving to God.

entries.author: The Blessed Bible Study Guide
entries.text:
**Paul's Defense of His Ministry**

**Themes:** Spiritual Warfare, Apostolic Authority, Boasting in the Lord

**Outline:**
I. Paul Defends His Authority (10:1-11)
II. Proper Boasting (10:12-18)

**Summary:**
Paul shifts his tone, defending his apostolic authority against critics who say his letters are weighty but his presence is weak. He explains that his weapons are not worldly but have divine power to demolish strongholds. He criticizes those who commend themselves by comparing themselves to others, asserting that any boasting should only be in the Lord.

entries.author: The Blessed Bible Study Guide
entries.text:
**Paul and the False Apostles**

**Themes:** Godly Jealousy, False Apostles, Suffering for Christ

**Outline:**
I. Paul's Godly Jealousy (11:1-6)
II. Paul's Support in Ministry (11:7-15)
III. Paul's Sufferings as an Apostle (11:16-33)

**Summary:**
Paul expresses a 'godly jealousy' for the Corinthians, fearing they are being led astray by 'super-apostles' preaching a different Jesus. He exposes these false apostles as deceitful workers masquerading as servants of righteousness. He then reluctantly 'boasts' in his weaknesses, cataloging his extensive sufferings, beatings, shipwrecks, and daily anxieties for the churches.

entries.author: The Blessed Bible Study Guide
entries.text:
**Paul's Vision and Thorn in the Flesh**

**Themes:** Visions, Weakness, Grace, Concern for the Corinthian Church

**Outline:**
I. Paul's Vision of Paradise (12:1-6)
II. The Thorn in the Flesh (12:7-10)
III. Paul's Concern for the Corinthians (12:11-21)

**Summary:**
Paul describes a vision where he was caught up to the third heaven. To keep him from becoming conceited, he was given a 'thorn in the flesh.' Despite pleading for its removal, God answered, 'My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness.' Paul expresses concern that upon his next visit, he may find them unrepentant of sin.

entries.author: The Blessed Bible Study Guide
entries.text:
**Final Warnings and Greetings**

**Themes:** Self-Examination, Restoration, Apostolic Authority, Trinitarian Blessing

**Outline:**
I. Final Warnings (13:1-4)
II. Call to Self-Examination (13:5-10)
III. Final Greetings and Benediction (13:11-14)

**Summary:**
Preparing for his third visit, Paul warns that he will not spare those who have sinned. He urges the Corinthians to examine themselves to see whether they are in the faith. He expresses his hope that they will do what is right. He concludes the letter with final exhortations to strive for full restoration and offers a beautiful Trinitarian benediction.

entries.author: The Blessed Bible Study Guide
entries.text:
**The Beginning of the Gospel**

**Themes:** John the Baptist, Baptism of Jesus, Temptation, Calling Disciples, Miracles and Authority

**Outline:**
I. John the Baptist Prepares the Way (1:1-8)
II. The Baptism and Temptation of Jesus (1:9-13)
III. Jesus Calls the First Disciples (1:14-20)
IV. Jesus Heals and Casts out Demons (1:21-45)

**Summary:**
The Gospel of Mark opens rapidly with the ministry of John the Baptist, followed by Jesus' baptism, temptation, and the launch of His public ministry in Galilee, marked by teaching with authority, calling disciples, and performing miraculous healings and exorcisms.

entries.author: The Blessed Bible Study Guide
entries.text:
**Jesus' Authority to Forgive Sins**

**Themes:** Forgiveness, Conflict with Religious Leaders, Fasting, Lord of the Sabbath

**Outline:**
I. Jesus Forgives and Heals a Paralyzed Man (2:1-12)
II. Jesus Calls Levi and Eats with Sinners (2:13-17)
III. Questions About Fasting (2:18-22)
IV. Jesus is Lord of the Sabbath (2:23-28)

**Summary:**
Jesus demonstrates His divine authority to forgive sins by healing a paralyzed man, leading to rising opposition from religious leaders. Conflicts escalate over His association with sinners, His disciples' lack of fasting, and His interpretation of the Sabbath.

entries.author: The Blessed Bible Study Guide
entries.text:
**Appointing the Twelve Apostles**

**Themes:** Healing on the Sabbath, The Twelve Apostles, The Unforgivable Sin, Jesus' True Family

**Outline:**
I. Healing a Man's Shriveled Hand on the Sabbath (3:1-6)
II. Crowds Follow Jesus (3:7-12)
III. Appointing the Twelve Apostles (3:13-19)
IV. Jesus Accused by His Family and Teachers of the Law (3:20-30)
V. Jesus' Mother and Brothers (3:31-35)

**Summary:**
Opposition intensifies after Jesus heals on the Sabbath. He selects twelve apostles to share in His ministry, faces accusations from religious leaders of being possessed by Beelzebul, and redefines His true family as those who do God's will.

entries.author: The Blessed Bible Study Guide
entries.text:
**Parables of the Kingdom**

**Themes:** The Parable of the Sower, The Purpose of Parables, Faith and Fear, Jesus' Power over Nature

**Outline:**
I. The Parable of the Sower (4:1-20)
II. A Lamp on a Stand (4:21-25)
III. The Parable of the Growing Seed (4:26-29)
IV. The Parable of the Mustard Seed (4:30-34)
V. Jesus Calms the Storm (4:35-41)

**Summary:**
Jesus teaches the crowds through parables, focusing on the Parable of the Sower to illustrate the varied responses to the word of God. Later, He demonstrates His absolute authority over nature by calming a severe storm on the Sea of Galilee, astonishing His disciples.

entries.author: The Blessed Bible Study Guide
entries.text:
**Miracles of Healing and Restoration**

**Themes:** Demon Possession, Faith and Healing, Power over Death

**Outline:**
I. Jesus Restores a Demon-Possessed Man (5:1-20)
II. Jesus Raises Jairus' Daughter and Heals a Bleeding Woman (5:21-43)

**Summary:**
Jesus continues to display His power by casting a legion of demons out of a man, healing a woman who had bled for twelve years simply through her faith-filled touch, and raising the young daughter of Jairus from the dead.

entries.author: The Blessed Bible Study Guide
entries.text:
**Rejection and Sending Out the Twelve**

**Themes:** Rejection at Nazareth, Sending the Apostles, Death of John the Baptist, Feeding the 5,000, Walking on Water

**Outline:**
I. A Prophet Without Honor (6:1-6)
II. Jesus Sends Out the Twelve (6:7-13)
III. John the Baptist Beheaded (6:14-29)
IV. Jesus Feeds the Five Thousand (6:30-44)
V. Jesus Walks on the Water (6:45-56)

**Summary:**
Jesus faces rejection in His hometown of Nazareth. He commissions the Twelve for ministry. The tragic death of John the Baptist is recounted, followed by Jesus miraculously feeding five thousand people and walking on water, though the disciples struggle to understand.

entries.author: The Blessed Bible Study Guide
entries.text:
**Inner Purity and Ministry to Gentiles**

**Themes:** Tradition of the Elders, Inner Purity, Faith of Gentiles

**Outline:**
I. That Which Defiles (7:1-23)
II. Jesus Honors a Syrophoenician Woman's Faith (7:24-30)
III. Jesus Heals a Deaf and Mute Man (7:31-37)

**Summary:**
Jesus confronts the Pharisees over their hypocritical reliance on human traditions regarding purity, teaching that defilement comes from the heart. He then ministers in Gentile territories, healing the daughter of a Syrophoenician woman and a deaf man.

entries.author: The Blessed Bible Study Guide
entries.text:
**Peter's Confession and the Cost of Discipleship**

**Themes:** Feeding the 4,000, The Yeast of the Pharisees, Peter's Confession, Prediction of the Passion

**Outline:**
I. Jesus Feeds the Four Thousand (8:1-13)
II. The Yeast of the Pharisees and Herod (8:14-21)
III. Healing a Blind Man at Bethsaida (8:22-26)
IV. Peter Declares That Jesus is the Messiah (8:27-30)
V. Jesus Predicts His Death (8:31-38)

**Summary:**
After feeding four thousand, Jesus warns against the influence of the Pharisees. Peter explicitly confesses Jesus as the Messiah. Jesus then predicts His impending death and resurrection, teaching that true discipleship requires taking up one's cross.

entries.author: The Blessed Bible Study Guide
entries.text:
**The Transfiguration and True Greatness**

**Themes:** The Transfiguration, Healing a Boy with an Impure Spirit, Servant Leadership

**Outline:**
I. The Transfiguration (9:1-13)
II. Jesus Heals a Boy Possessed by an Impure Spirit (9:14-29)
III. Jesus Predicts His Death a Second Time (9:30-32)
IV. Whoever is Not Against Us is For Us (9:33-41)
V. Causing to Stumble (9:42-50)

**Summary:**
Jesus is transfigured before Peter, James, and John, revealing His divine glory. Coming down the mountain, He heals a demon-possessed boy His disciples could not. He predicts His death again and redefines greatness as humble servanthood.

entries.author: The Blessed Bible Study Guide
entries.text:
**Teaching on Marriage, Wealth, and Servanthood**

**Themes:** Divorce, Little Children, The Rich Young Man, The Request of James and John, Healing Bartimaeus

**Outline:**
I. Divorce (10:1-12)
II. The Little Children and Jesus (10:13-16)
III. The Rich and the Kingdom of God (10:17-31)
IV. Jesus Predicts His Death a Third Time (10:32-34)
V. The Request of James and John (10:35-45)
VI. Blind Bartimaeus Receives His Sight (10:46-52)

**Summary:**
Jesus teaches about the permanence of marriage, welcomes little children, and warns about the spiritual danger of wealth through the rich young ruler. He predicts His passion a third time, counters the disciples' ambition by modeling servanthood, and heals blind Bartimaeus.

entries.author: The Blessed Bible Study Guide
entries.text:
**The Triumphal Entry and Cleansing the Temple**

**Themes:** The Triumphal Entry, Cursing the Fig Tree, Cleansing the Temple, Authority of Jesus

**Outline:**
I. Jesus Comes to Jerusalem as King (11:1-11)
II. Jesus Curses a Fig Tree and Clears the Temple Courts (11:12-19)
III. The Withered Fig Tree (11:20-26)
IV. The Authority of Jesus Questioned (11:27-33)

**Summary:**
Jesus enters Jerusalem to shouts of 'Hosanna,' symbolically curses a barren fig tree, and drives the merchants out of the temple courts. His actions prompt the religious leaders to question His authority, which He brilliantly evades.

entries.author: The Blessed Bible Study Guide
entries.text:
**Controversies in Jerusalem**

**Themes:** Parable of the Tenants, Paying Taxes to Caesar, Marriage at the Resurrection, The Greatest Commandment, The Widow's Offering

**Outline:**
I. The Parable of the Tenants (12:1-12)
II. Paying Taxes to Caesar (12:13-17)
III. Marriage at the Resurrection (12:18-27)
IV. The Greatest Commandment (12:28-34)
V. Whose Son Is the Messiah? (12:35-40)
VI. The Widow's Offering (12:41-44)

**Summary:**
Jesus tells the parable of the wicked tenants to indict the religious leaders. He navigates trap questions about taxes and the resurrection, identifies the greatest commandments as love for God and neighbor, and praises the sacrificial giving of a poor widow.

entries.author: The Blessed Bible Study Guide
entries.text:
**The Olivet Discourse**

**Themes:** Destruction of the Temple, Signs of the End of the Age, The Day and Hour Unknown

**Outline:**
I. The Destruction of the Temple and Signs of the End Times (13:1-23)
II. The Return of the Son of Man (13:24-27)
III. The Day and Hour Unknown (13:28-37)

**Summary:**
Jesus predicts the total destruction of the temple and gives a prophetic discourse on the Mount of Olives regarding the signs of the end of the age, severe tribulations, the return of the Son of Man, and the urgent need for believers to remain watchful.

entries.author: The Blessed Bible Study Guide
entries.text:
**The Last Supper, Betrayal, and Arrest**

**Themes:** Anointing at Bethany, The Last Supper, Gethsemane, Betrayal, Peter's Denial

**Outline:**
I. Jesus Anointed at Bethany (14:1-11)
II. The Lord's Supper (14:12-26)
III. Jesus Predicts Peter's Denial (14:27-31)
IV. Gethsemane (14:32-42)
V. Jesus Arrested (14:43-52)
VI. Jesus Before the Sanhedrin (14:53-65)
VII. Peter Disowns Jesus (14:66-72)

**Summary:**
The plot to kill Jesus unfolds as He is anointed for burial, celebrates the Last Supper, and agonizes in Gethsemane. Judas betrays Him, leading to His arrest and a late-night trial before the Sanhedrin, while Peter tragically denies knowing Him three times.

entries.author: The Blessed Bible Study Guide
entries.text:
**The Trial, Crucifixion, and Burial**

**Themes:** Trial Before Pilate, The Crucifixion, The Death of Jesus, The Burial

**Outline:**
I. Jesus Before Pilate (15:1-15)
II. The Soldiers Mock Jesus (15:16-20)
III. The Crucifixion of Jesus (15:21-32)
IV. The Death of Jesus (15:33-41)
V. The Burial of Jesus (15:42-47)

**Summary:**
Jesus is tried by Pontius Pilate, who condemns Him to be crucified to placate the crowd. He is mocked by soldiers, crucified at Golgotha, and dies on the cross, after which Joseph of Arimathea boldly requests His body for a dignified burial.

entries.author: The Blessed Bible Study Guide
entries.text:
**The Resurrection**

**Themes:** The Empty Tomb, The Resurrection, Appearances of Jesus, The Great Commission

**Outline:**
I. Jesus Has Risen (16:1-8)
II. Jesus Appears to Mary Magdalene and Disciples (16:9-14)
III. The Great Commission and Ascension (16:15-20)

**Summary:**
Women visit the tomb on Sunday morning to find it empty and receive an angelic message that Jesus has risen. The ending recounts His appearances to His followers, the commissioning of the disciples to preach the gospel globally, and His ascension into heaven.

entries.author: Ellen G. White
entries.text: ]IS name shall be called Immanuel, . . . God with us." "The light of the knowledge of the glory of God" is seen "in the face of Jesus Christ." From the days of eternity the Lord Jesus Christ was one with the Father; He was "the image of God," the image of His greatness and majesty, "the outshining of His glory." It was to manifest this glory that He came to our world. To this sin-darkened earth He came to reveal the light of God's love, — to be "God with us." Therefore it was prophesied of Him, "His name shall be called Immanuel." By coming to dwell with us, Jesus was to reveal God both to men and to angels. He was the Word of God, — God's thought made audible. In His prayer for His disciples He says, "I have declared unto them Thy name/' — "merciful and gracious, longsuffering, and abundant in goodness and truth/' — "that the love wherewith Thou hast loved Me may be in them, and I in them." But not alone for His earth-born children was this revelation given. Our little world is the lesson-book of the universe. God's wonderful purpose of grace, the mystery of 2 (17) i8 redeeming love, is the theme into which "angels desire to look," and it will.be their study throughout endless ages. Both the redeemed and the unfallen beings will find in the cross of Christ their science and their song. It will be seen that the glory shining in the face of Jesus is the glory of self-sacrificing love. In the light from Calvary it will be seen, that the law of self- renouncing love is the law of life for earth and heaven; that the love which "seeketh not her own" has its source in the heart of God; and that in the meek and lowly One is manifested the character of Him who dwelleth in. the light which no man can approach unto. Angels "find in the cross of Christ their science and their song." In the beginning, God was revealed in all the works of creation. It was Christ that spread the heavens, and laid the foundations of the earth. It was His hand that hung the worlds in space, and fashioned the flowers ' of the field. "His strength setteth fast the mountains." "The sea, is His, and He made it"1 It was He that filled the earth with beauty, and the air with song. And upon all things in earth, and air, and sky, He wrote the message of the Father's love. Now sin has marred God's perfect work, yet that handwriting; remains. Even now all created things declare the glory of His excellence. There is nothing, save the selfish heart of man, that lives unto itself. No bird that cleaves the air, no animal that moves upon the ground, but ministers to some other life. There is no leaf of the forest, or lowly blade of grass, but has its ministry. Every tree and shrub and leaf pours forth ips. 65:6; 95:5. GOD WITH US. that element of life, without which neither man nor animal could live; and man and animal, in turn, minister to the life of tree and shrub and leaf. The flowers breathe fragrance and unfold their beauty in blessing to the world. The sun sheds its light to gladden a thousand worlds. The ocean, itself the source of all our springs and fountains, receives the streams from every land, but takes to give. The mists ascending from its bosom fall in showers to water the earth, that it may bring forth and bud. The angels of glory find their joy in giving, — giving" love and tireless watch- care to souls that are fallen and unholy. Heavenly beings woo the hearts of men; they bring to this dark world light from the courts above; by gentle and patient ministry they move upon the human spirit, to bring the lost into a fellowship with Christ which is even closer than they themselves can know. But turning from all lesser repre- sentations, we behold God in Jesus. Looking unto Jesus we see that it is the glory of our God to give. "I do nothing of Myself/' said Christ; "the living Father hath sent Me, and I live by the Father/' "I seek not Mine own glory," but the glory of Him that sent Me.1 In these words is set forth the great principle which is the law of life for the universe. All things Christ received from God, but He took to give. So in the heavenly courts, in His min- istry for all created beings: through the beloved Son, the Father's life flows out to all; through the Son ft returns, in praise and joyous service, a tide of love, to the great Source of all. ' And thus through Christ the circuit of beneficence is complete, representing the character of the great Giver, the law of life. 1 John 8:28; 6:57; 8:50; 7:18. "He deceived angels, • - . and the night of Woe settled down upon tKe World," Page 20. 2Q In heaven itself this law was broken. Sin originated in serf-seeking. Lucifer, the covering cherub, desired to be first in heaven. He sought to gain control of heavenly beings, to draw them away from their Creator, and to win their homage to himself. Therefore he misrepresented God, attributing to Him the desire for self-exaltation With his own evil characteristics he sought to invest the loving Creator. Thus he deceived angels. Thus he deceived men. He led them to doubt the word of God, and to distrust His goodness. Because God is a God of justice and terrible majesty, Satan caused them to look upon Him as severe and unforgiving. Thus he drew men to join him in rebellion against God, and the night of woe settled down upon the world. The earth was dark through misapprehension of God. That the gloomy shadows might be lightened, that the world might be brought back to God, Satan's deceptive power was to be broken. This could not be done by force The exercise of force is contrary to the principles of God's government; He desires only the service of love; and love cannot be commanded; it cannot be won by force or authority. Only by love is love awakened To know God is to love Him; His character must be manifested in contrast to the character of Satan. This work only one Being in all the universe could do. Only He who knew the height and depth of the love of God, could make it known. Upon the world's dark night the Sun of Righteousness must rise, "with healing in His wings."1 The plan for our redemption was not an after-thought, a plan form- ulated after the fall of Adam. It was a revelation of "the mystery which hath been kept in silence through times eternal."2 It was an unfolding- of the principles that from eternal ages have been the foundation of God's throne. From the beginning, God and Christ knew of the apostasy of Satan, and of the fall of man through the deceptive power of the apostate. God did not ordain that sin should exist, but He foresaw its existence, and made provision to meet the terrible emergency. So great was His love for the world, that He covenanted to give His only begotten Son, "that whosoever believeth in Him should not perish, but have everlasting life."8 Lucifer had said, "I will exalt my throne above the stars of God; ... I will be like the Most High,"4 But Christ, "being in the form of God, counted it not a thing to be grasped to be on an equality with God, but emptied Himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men."6 1Mal. 4:2. 2Rom. 16:25, R. V. 8John 3:16. *Isa. 14:13, 14. 5 Phil. 2:6, 7, R. V., margin. GOD WITH US. 21 This was a voluntary sacrifice. Jesus might have remained at the Father's side. He might have retained the glory of heaven, and the homage of the angels. But He chose to give back the scepter into the Father's hands, and to step down from the throne of the universe, that He might bring light to the benighted, and life to the perishing. Nearly two thousand years ago, a voice of mysterious import was heard in heaven, from the throne of God, "Lo, I come " . "Sacrifice and offering Thou wouldst not, but a body hast Thou prepared Me Lo, I come (in the volume of the book it is written of Me,) to do Thy will, O God "* In these words is announced the fulfilment of the purpose that had been hidden from eternal ages. Christ was about to visit our world, and to become incarnate. He says, "A body hast Thou prepared Me." Had He appeared with the glory that was His with the Father before the world was, we could not have endured the light of His presence. That we might behold it and not be destroyed, the manifestation of His glory was shrouded. His divinity was veiled with humanity, — the invisible glory in the visible human form. This great purpose had been shadowed forth in types and symbols. The burning bush, in which Christ appeared to Moses, revealed God The symbol chosen for the representation of the Deity was a lowly shrub, that seemingly had no attractions. This enshnned the Infinite. The all-merciful God shrouded His glory in a most humble type, that Moses could look upon it and live So in the pillar of cloud by day and the pillar of fire by night, God communicated with Israel, revealing to men His will, and imparting to them His grace. God's glory was subdued, and His majesty veiled, that the weak vision of finite men might behold it. So Christ was to come in "the body of our humilia- tion,"2 "in the likeness of men" In the eyes of the world He possessed no beauty that they should desire Him; yet He was the incarnate God, the light of heaven and earth. His glory was veiled, His greatness and majesty were hidden, that He might draw near to sorrowful, tempted men. God commanded Moses for Israel, "Let them make Me a sanctuary, that I may dwell anrong them,"3 and He abode in the sanctuary, in the midst of His people Through all their weary wandering in the desert, the symbol of His presence was with them. So Christ set up His tabernacle in the midst of our human encampment. He pitched His tent by the side of the tents of men, that He might dwell among us, and make us familiar with His divine character and life. "The Word became 1 Heb. 10 : 5-7. 2 ™1. 3 : 21, R. V. 3Ex. 25 : 8. 22 flesh, and tabernacled among us (and we beheld His glory, glory as of the only begotten from the Father) full of grace and truth"1 Since Jesus came to dwell with us, we know that God is acquainted with our trials, and sympathizes with our griefs. Every son and daughter of Adam may understand that our Creator is the friend of sinners. For in every doctrine of grace, every promise of joy, every deed of love, every divine attraction presented in the Saviour's life on earth, we see "God with us " -Satan represents God's law of love as a law of selfishness. He declares that it is impossible for us to obey its precepts, The fall of our first parents, with all the woe that has resulted, he charges upon the Creator, leading men to look upon God as the author of sin, and suffering, and death. Jesus was to unveil this deception. As one of us He was to give an example of ofeedience. For this He took upon Himself our nature, and passed through our experiences, "In all things it behooved Him to be made like unto His brethren."2 If we had to bear anything which Jesus did not endure, then upon this point Satan would represent the power of God as insufficient for us. Therefore Jesus was "in all points tempted like as we are "3 He endured every trial to which we are subject. And He exercised in His own behalf no power that is not freely offered to us. As man, He met temptation, and overcame in the strength given Him from God. He says, "I delight to do Thy will, O My God; yea, Thy law is within My heart "* As He went about doing good, and healing all who were afflicted by Satan, He made plain to men the character of God's law and the nature of His service. His life testifies that it is possible for us also to obey the law of God By His humanity, Christ touched humanity; by His divinity, He lays hold upon the throne of God As the Son of man, He gavet us an example of obedience; as the Son of God, He gives us power to obey. It was Christ who from the bush on Mount Horeb spoke to Moses saying, "I AM THAT I AM. . . . \ Thus shalt thou say unto the children of Israel, I AM hath sent me unto you."5 This was the pledge of Israel's deliverance. So when He came "in the likeness of men," He declared Himself the I AM. The Child of Bethlehem, the meek and lowly Saviour, is God "manifest in the flesh"6 And to us He says, '"I AM the Good Shepherd/ 'I AM the living Bread' 'I AM the Way, the Truth, and the Life.' 'All power is given unto Me in heaven 1 John r . 14, R. V , margin. 2 Heb 2 : 17. s Heb. 4 : 15. * Ps. 40 : 8. 5 Ex. 3:14. 6i Tim. 3:16. GOD WITH US. 25 and in earth.'1 'I AM the assurance of every promise* *I AM; be not afraid'" "God with us" is the surety of our deliverance from sin, the assurance of our power to obey the law of heaven. In stooping to take upon Himself humanity, Christ revealed a char- acter the opposite of the character of Satan. But He stepped still lower m. the path of humiliation "Being found in fashion as a man, He humbled Himself, and became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross."2 As the high priest laid aside his gorgeous pontifical robes, and officiated in the white linen dress of the common priest, so Christ took the form of a servant, and offered sacrifice, Himself the priest, Himself the victim. fe^He^was wounded for our transgressions, He was bruised for our iniquities; the chastisement of our peace was upon Him."3 Christ was treated as we deserve, that we might be treated as He deserves. He was condemned for our sins, in which He had no share, that we might be justified by His righteousness, in which we had no share. He suffered the death which was ours, that we might receive the life which was His. "With His stripes we are healed" By His life and His death, Christ has achieved even more than recovery from the ruin wrought through sin. It was Satan's purpose to bring about an eternal separation between God and man, but in Christ we become more closely united to God than if we had never fallen. In taking our nature, the Saviour has bound Himself to humanity by a tie that is never to be broken. Through the eternal ages He is linked with us. "God so loved the world, that He gave His only begotten Son."4 He gave Him not only to bear our sins, and to die as our sacrifice; He gave Him to the fallen race. To assure us of His immutable counsel of peace, God gave His only begotten Son to become one of the human family, forever to retain His human nature. This is the pledge that God will fulfil His word. {"Unto ^a^child is born; unto us a son is given; and the government shall be upon His shoulder." God has adopted human nature in the person of His Son, and has carried the same into the highest heaven. It is the "Son of man" who shares the throne of the universe It is the "Son of man" whose name shall be called, "Wonderful, Counselor, the mighty God, the everlasting Father, the Prince of Peace."5 The I AM is the Daysman between God and humanity, laying His hand upon both. He who is "holy, harmless, undefiled, separate from sinners," is not ashamed to call us brethren.6 In Christ the family of earth and the family of heaven are 'John 10:11; 6:51; 14:6; Matt. 28:18. 2Phil. 2:8. 3Isa. 53'5- *John 3:16. sisa. 9:6. 6Heb. 7:26; 2:11. 26 bound together. Christ glorified is our brother. Heaven is enshrined in humanity, and humanity is enfolded in the bosom of Infinite Love. Of His people God says, "They shall be as the stones of a crown, lifted up as an ensign upon His land. For how great is His goodness, and how great is His beauty!"1 The exaltation of the redeemed will be an eternal testimony to God's mercy. "In the ages to come," He will "show the exceeding riches of His grace in His kindness toward us through Christ Jesus." "To the intent that . . . unto the principalities and the powers in the heavenly places might be made known . . . the manifold wisdom of God, according to the eternal purpose which He purposed in Christ Jesus our Lord."2 Through Christ's redeeming work the government of God stands justified. The Omnipotent One is made known as the God of love. Satan's charges are refuted, and his character unveiled. Rebellion can never again arise. Sin can never again enter the universe. Through eternal ages all are secure from apostasy. By love's self-sacrifice, the inhabitants of earth and heaven are bound to their Creator in bonds of indissoluble union. The work of redemption will be complete. In the place where sin abounded, God's grace much more abounds. The earth itself, the very field that Satan claims as his, is to be not only ransomed but exalted. Our little world, under the curse of sin the one dark blot in His glorious creation, will be honored above all other worlds in the universe of God. Here, where the Son of God tabernacled in humanity; where the King of Glory lived and suffered and died, — here, when He shall make all things new, the tabernacle of God shall be with men, ^ and He shall dwell with them, and they shall be His people, and God Himself shall be with them? and be their God.'* And through endless ages as the redeemed walk in the light of the Lord, they will praise Him for His unspeakable Gift, — Immanuel, "God with us/' iZech. 9:16, 17. 2Eph. 2:7; 3:10, ii, R. V.

entries.author: Ellen G. White
entries.text: "OR more than a thousand years the Jewish people had awaited the Saviour's coming. Upon this event they had rested their brightest hopes. In song and prophecy, in temple rite and household prayer, they had enshrined His name. And yet at His coming, they knew Him not. The Beloved of heaven was .to them "as a root out of a dry ground;1' He had "no form nor comeliness;" and they saw in Him no beauty that they should desire Him. "He came unto His own, and His own received Him not."1 Yet God had chosen Israel. He had called them to preserve among men the knowledge of His law, and of the symbols and prophecies that pointed to the Saviour. He desired them to be as wells of salvation to the world. What Abraham was in the land of his sojourn, what Joseph was in Egypt, and Daniel in the. courts of Babylon, the Hebrew people were to be among the nations. They were to reveal God to men. In the call of Abraham. the Lord had said, "I will bless thee, and thou shalt be a blessing, . . . and in thee shall all families of the earth be blessed." 2 The same teaching was repeated through the prophets.
